tier_rationale: The Pinecil V2's Bouffalo BL706 chip includes Bluetooth Low Energy hardware, and IronOS -- the open-source firmware it ships with as the stock, out-of-box experience -- lists BLE as a supported feature on Pinecil V2 in its current stable release. PINE64 operates no account system, app store, or cloud service of any kind for the iron: BLE is used only for local, in-room communication with a phone or PC, so the radio's presence puts this at D1 rather than D0, with no vendor cloud in the picture to make it D2.
the_unplug_test: There is nothing to unplug from. The Pinecil is a USB-C/barrel-jack powered soldering iron, configured and used entirely from its own on-device menu and OLED screen; the only thing on the network is your own room, if you choose to pair the BLE radio to a phone at all. Every setting -- temperature, sleep behavior, power source negotiation -- lives in the iron itself and in the open-source IronOS firmware you flash onto it over USB, not in any account.

repairability.notes: PINE64 sells individual replacement parts directly (shell halves, DC jack, breakout board, tips) and the hardware schematics are published openly.

sources.supports: Manufacturer's own store listing for the Pinecil V2: community price $25.99 / retail $35.99, chipset Bouffalo BL-706, OS listed as 'Ralim's IronOS build,' certifications FCC/CE RED/ROHS, and no account, app, or cloud service named anywhere in setup or use.

The official IronOS firmware repository's supported-hardware table lists Pinecil V2 with BLE marked as supported in the current stable release (v2.23), and states the firmware is installed by flashing over USB from a downloaded release -- confirming both the radio's functional presence and that firmware updates are a manual, ownership-controlled action rather than a forced over-the-air push.

PINE64's own wiki: 'The v2 model allows BLE Bluetooth control because of the switch to the Bouffalo BL706 MCU... The BL706 features Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE / Zigbee); future IronOS firmware releases will expose features over BLE,' and separately states the Pinecil running 'the newest official GitHub IronOS firmware' is the authentic, stock configuration -- i.e. open firmware is not a liberation step here, it is what ships.

open_questions: PINE64's own filed FCC compliance document for the Pinecil V2 (https://files.pine64.org/doc/cert/Pinecilv2%20FCC%20Certificate%20LCSA070722057E.pdf, dated 22 July 2022, at Pinecil V2's original launch) covers only FCC Part 15 Subpart B (unintentional-radiator emissions, Class B SDoC) and lists no FCC ID or Part 15C intentional-radiator grant for the BLE radio. This is genuinely inconsistent with the chip-level and firmware-level BLE documentation cited above; it may mean BLE was not yet enabled in shipped firmware at the time of that filing (IronOS's own wiki text calls BLE a 'future' firmware feature as of the V2 launch) and a fuller radiator certification was filed later but not located, or it may be a real compliance gap. Flagged rather than resolved: it does not change what the hardware does, but a maintainer may want to note it.

Exactly what functions IronOS currently exposes over BLE (read-only telemetry vs. settings changes) and whether any third-party companion app exists were not confirmed beyond the firmware repo's support-table checkmark.
PINE64 as a company/vendor is not in data/vendors.json; a light search turned up no incident of a PINE64 device losing function post-purchase, but the check was not exhaustive.
notes: The soldering-station answer to the brief's question 'does open-by-default make this D0 with a liberation story, or something else': it's something else. Because the V2 hardware includes a working BLE radio, D0 ('no radio') does not literally apply even though the device is about as vendor-independent as hardware gets -- PINE64 sells the iron, publishes the schematics, and the stock firmware is the same open-source project (Ralim's IronOS) that a liberation effort would install on a closed competitor. D3's liberation field was left null because D3 only applies to devices that are cloud-dependent as sold; this one was never cloud-dependent, so there is nothing to liberate it from.
